evidence.command: sed -n '35,45p;65,75p' Cargo.toml | grep -vE '^\s*$|^#' && sed -n '37,47p' crates/cobre-solver/Cargo.toml && sed -n '35,45p' crates/cobre-comm/Cargo.toml && sed -n '46,56p' crates/cobre-python/Cargo.toml

expect_used = "warn"

unwrap_used = "deny"
expect_used = "warn"
panic = "warn"
too_many_arguments = "deny"
--- python (5 of 6; the table ends here)
unwrap_used = "deny"
expect_used = "warn"
panic = "warn"
evidence.reading: Both station replicas are faithful at this baseline — 6 of 6 clippy entries and both rust entries, with only `unsafe_code` flipped from `forbid` to `allow`, which FFI and the `unsafe impl Send/Sync` justify and which is not what this candidate is about. The third replica is the proof that the mechanism, not the current text, is the defect: crates/cobre-python/Cargo.toml carries 5 of 6 and is missing `too_many_arguments = "deny"`. That instance is the cli-python station's to raise; cited here only to show the hand-copy has already drifted once. The drift direction matters for severity: dropping a `deny` removes a check, so the drifted crate builds green and no gate anywhere in CI compares the three tables against the workspace table.

candidates.fixShape: The Cargo constraint is real — a manifest cannot combine `lints.workspace = true` with a per-lint override — so the fix is not deduplication but making the copies checkable, and there are two shapes with a genuine trade-off for the owner. First shape, three copies and one guard: add a CI check that parses the workspace `[workspace.lints.*]` tables and each replicating manifest and asserts set equality modulo one declared exception list (today: `unsafe_code`), failing on any key present in the workspace table and absent from a replica. This keeps `forbid` at the workspace root, costs one script, and turns a silent omission into a red build; its weakness is that the exception list is itself hand-maintained. Second shape, remove the reason the copies exist: downgrade the workspace `unsafe_code` from `forbid` to `deny`, let all three crates carry plain `lints.workspace = true`, and have each FFI crate re-admit unsafe at its own crate root with a scoped `expect` carrying the justification next to the code it licenses. That leaves exactly one table in the workspace and no drift surface at all, at the cost of `forbid`'s property that no crate can override it — the guarantee becomes per-crate-auditable rather than structurally impossible. Blast radius of the first is one new CI job and no manifest edits; of the second, three manifests plus one crate-root attribute per FFI crate, and an owner decision about giving up `forbid`. Severity is B rather than C because the observable failure is a lint that silently stops running.

candidates.title: The CLP per-element basis code space has four spellings and no owner, and the comment that forbids a symbolic definition rests on a premise the code contradicts

evidence.command: git show 077dbe2c:crates/cobre-solver/src/basis_status.rs | awk 'NR>=9&&NR<=12||NR>=67&&NR<=75{printf "%d:%s\n",NR,$0}' && git show 077dbe2c:crates/cobre-solver/src/ffi/clp.rs | awk 'NR>=29&&NR<=31{printf "%d:%s\n",NR,$0}' && git grep -n 'CLP_BASIS' 077dbe2c -- crates/cobre-solver/src
evidence.reading: The same six-value CLP code space is written out in four places at this baseline: the C header contract (csrc/clp_wrapper.h:209-210), the ffi/clp.rs:27-31 comment, bare literals in both directions of the canonical mapping (basis_status.rs:69-74 and 84-89), and two named private constants covering two of the six values in a third module (backends/clp/solver.rs:18,22, used at :290 and :299). The comment's premise is false: the codes are not round-tripped verbatim — they are decoded into the canonical enum at backends/clp/interface.rs:624,632 and re-encoded at backends/clp/solver.rs:250,264, with folding (`Nonbasic` and `Superbasic` both leave as 4), so the numerals are interpreted, not passed through. The comment nonetheless uses that premise to justify keeping no symbolic definition, which is precisely why the numerals ended up spread across three Rust modules. The asymmetry is visible in one screen: the HiGHS half of the very same enum imports its five codes as named constants from the binding module (basis_status.rs:9-12) and is therefore anchored to the header by the compiler, while the CLP half is anchored to nothing. The dangling reference at backends/clp/interface.rs:600 shows the cost already landing on readers: it documents the mapping as being over `CLP_BASIS_*` codes, but that family exists only in a different module and covers only two of the six values, so nothing at the documented site resolves.

candidates.fixShape: Give the CLP code space one owner in the binding module, mirroring what the HiGHS side already does: declare all six values as named constants in ffi/clp.rs next to the header they mirror, have both directions of the canonical mapping match on those names instead of bare numerals, and have the two private constants in backends/clp/solver.rs use them rather than redeclare two of the six. Rewrite the ffi/clp.rs:27-31 rationale to say what is true — the codes are interpreted in both directions, so they get names — instead of the round-tripped-verbatim premise that argued against naming them. Then backends/clp/interface.rs:600's `CLP_BASIS_*` reference resolves to something real, and the numerals stop being duplicated across three modules. This is a two-way door with no public surface change: the mapping functions keep their signatures, so the blast radius is one binding module, one enum body, and two constants. It is worth doing above C severity because the numerals are a warm-start correctness contract — a value transposed in one of the three copies mis-installs a basis silently rather than failing to compile — and because a future sixth-value change today has to be found in four places, one of which actively tells the reader not to look for names.

candidates.title: Informational: the solver trait has no capability-query surface and exactly one backend compiles, so building the capability trait at this baseline would be a one-consumer abstraction

evidence.command: git show 077dbe2c:crates/cobre-solver/src/lib.rs | grep -nE 'compile_error|^pub\(crate\) mod ffi' && git show 077dbe2c:crates/cobre-solver/src/trait_def.rs | grep -nE 'pub trait SolverInterface|type Profile'
evidence.reading: Both-backends and no-backend are compile errors, so exactly one backend exists in any build and no caller can ask which one it is at run time. The trait's only backend-varying surface is the `Profile` associated type, deliberately constrained to `Copy + PartialEq + Default + Send` and documented at the declaration as opaque to backend-generic consumers, with cross-backend tuning intent belonging in a backend-agnostic hint. candidates.fixShape: Record and change nothing at this baseline. The capability surface should arrive with its second consumer, i.e. when two backends must coexist in one binary (roadmap III.6); at that point the trait grows the query a caller can branch on and the compile-time pair relaxes into a selection, and the abstraction has two implementations on the day it is written. Until then the `Profile` doc already states the correct rule for callers — treat it as opaque, put cross-backend tuning intent in a backend-agnostic hint — and the two compile errors are doing the job a capability query would otherwise do, at zero run-time cost. Any variant that builds the capability trait now has exactly one implementation and is speculative generality rather than architecture; if such a variant is proposed it should be tagged `conflicts` and held, with this record cited as the reason.
